newsitem.title: FRANCE: Heavy sentences sought in French graves attack.
newsitem.headline: Heavy sentences sought in French graves attack.

text.p: A French prosecutor in the trial of four neo-Nazis accused of desecrating a Jewish cemetery in southern France urged a court on Thursday to pass the maximum sentence on the two alleged ringleaders.

Prosecutor Fabienne Roze urged the court to sentence non-commissioned army officer Olivier Fimbry, 31, and Patrick Laonegro, 28, described as the ideologist of the group, to two years in jail for instigating the May 1990 attack on the centuries-old cemetery in the town of Carpentras.

"(Fimbry) could have made a good soldier if he had admired the French army instead of the Waffen SS," Roze told the court. "I can accept that Laonegro came up with the ideas but the others were far from passive."

The desecration, in which the recently buried body of Felix Germon was dug up, his sodomisation simulated with a beach umbrella, and 34 graves wrecked, provoked revulsion throughout France and the world.
It prompted hundreds of thousands of people to march in a protest led by late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.
Roze sought an 18-month jail term for Yannick Garnier, 27, whose confession last July led to the arrests of his suspected accomplices, and for Bertrand Nouveau, 28.
The defence was to make its pleas later in the day, with judgement due later this year.

All four defendants expressed remorse for the desecration in court earlier this week. But Fimbry and Laonegro said they still admired Nazi ideology while the other two said they had since abandoned fascist views.
"The question, six years later, is not the sincerity of the confessions, but the sincerity of the remorse," Roze said.
Garnier's confession capped a six-year investigation which had seemed to be leading nowhere.

At the time of their arrests, investigators said, all four accused were either members or sympathisers of the tiny Nationalist French and European Party which became known in the 1980s in connection with a series of attacks against Arab immigrations.
A fifth member of the group, Jean-Claude Gos, has since been killed in a motorcycle accident.
Lawyers for the civil plaintiffs blamed extreme right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen in court on Wednesday for encouraging the desecration by whipping up anti-Semitism in France.
Le Pen has repeatedly protested his innocence and complained of being the victim of a political witchhunt.
